Issued at 246 PM CDT Wed Sep 2 2026

Broad upper ridging continues to reside across the Ohio and 
Tennessee River Valleys and southern Great Lakes which is 
resulting in another hot and humid afternoon. Temperatures have 
continued to warm into the mid-90s and with dew points in the 
lower to mid-70s, heat indices are once again peaking in the 
100-105F range this afternoon. While the upper ridge is expected
to gradually drift south and east into the Mid-Atlantic region 
tonight into Thursday, the hot and humid conditions are forecast
to persist through Thursday afternoon. However, with more cloud
cover expected Thursday temperatures should be a few degrees 
cooler which in turn should limit peak heat indices into the 
95-105F range with the highest readings forecast to occur south 
of I-80. That said, where heat indices due break the 100 degree 
mark there will be the danger for heat related illnesses which 
is why the Heat Advisory has been extended through 9 PM CDT 
Thursday evening for our north-central IL counties and all of 
our northwest IN counties. Regardless, anyone with outdoor plans
and/or activities Thursday should use caution and remain 
hydrated. 

As the aforementioned ridging pushes south and east, the parade
of shortwave disturbances that are currently ongoing in IA and 
WI will begin to pivot into northern IL and northwest IN and 
result in periods of showers and thunderstorms. The first period
of shower/storm chances is late tonight into Thursday morning 
as the disturbance currently in IA pivots across southern WI and
northern IL and interacts with a sagging surface boundary. 
Given that the ridge will still mainly be in control it looks as
if the bulk of any showers/storms tonight will stay north of 
the IL-WI line. Though, if sufficient storm coverage can occur 
in WI and push an outflow into northern IL tonight then some 
isolated to widely scattered showers with embedded lightning 
could drift into portions of northern and northeast IL towards 
daybreak Thursday morning. 

Another shortwave disturbance is expected to pivot across 
northern IL and Northwest IN Thursday afternoon and evening 
which should result in another period of scattered showers and 
thunderstorms. While the environment looks primed with MLCAPE 
values around 2500 J/kg and dew points in the low to mid-70s, 
storm coverage continues to be a point of uncertainty given the 
weaker forcing and lingering effects of the ridge. That said, 
the greatest coverage (20-30%) is currently forecast to occur 
north of I-80 closer to the center of the disturbance which 
should further help to limit the extent of the aforementioned 
heat in these areas but if storms fail to materialize then 
higher heat indices may be seen further northward. Any storms 
that do develop will also have the potential to become severe 
given the 35-40 kts of shear present. Since most of the 
instability should be elevated it seems the main threats with 
any severe storms should be damaging winds and large hail, but 
will need to monitor the potential for supercell structures 
which could result in a localized tornado threat especially near
any remnant outflow boundaries. Because of this severe threat 
the Storm Prediction Center has maintained the marginal (level 1
of 5) risk for our entire area for Thursday afternoon and 
evening. 

Heading into Thursday night, yet another thunderstorm complex 
is forecast to develop in southern WI and begin to drift 
southward towards northern IL. If the environment is not fully 
disrupted by any afternoon storms and/or can recover, then this 
complex should be able to move into northern IL and eventually 
northwest IN after midnight Thursday night and linger into early
Friday morning. Despite the unfavorable diurnal time the 
complex will still have decent instability and wind shear to 
work with which may allow a threat for damaging winds and hail 
to persist into the night. Additionally, the complex will also 
be moving into a veering low- level jet over northern IL which 
may support an axis of training thunderstorms. Given the humid 
air mass these storms will be capable of torrential downpours 
which may result in instances of flooding especially if the 
storms train over urban areas. Right now it is unclear where 
exactly this complex will track and thus where the heaviest 
rainfall will occur, but it seems that somewhere in northern IL 
and/or northwest IN could see an area of 1-2+ inch rain amounts.

By Friday, another upper ridge is forecast to begin to build 
into the central CONUS which will generate northwest flow aloft 
over the Great Lakes. While this pattern will keep the periodic 
shower and thunderstorm chances in play through much of the 
upcoming holiday weekend, it does appear that the aforementioned
storm complex should work over the atmosphere enough to result 
in mostly dry conditions for at least the daylight hours Friday.
Our next period of showers and thunderstorms looks to develop
